'''''Tecoma stans''''' is a species of [[Flowering plant|flowering]] [[perennial]] [[shrub]] in the [[Campsis|trumpet vine]] family, [[Bignoniaceae]], that is native to the [[Americas]].  Common names include '''yellow trumpetbush''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date = 22 December 2017}}</ref> '''yellow bells''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''yellow elder''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''ginger Thomas'''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Plants – Buck Island Reef |url=https://www.nps.gov/buis/learn/nature/plants.htm |publisher=[[National Park Service]] (US) |access-date=19 January 2023}}</ref> ''Tecoma stans'' is the official flower of the [[United States Virgin Islands]] and the [[floral emblem]] of [[The Bahamas]].

==Description==
''Tecoma stans'' is a [[semi-evergreen]] shrub or small tree, growing up to {{cvt|10|m|-1}} tall.<ref name=IUCN/> It features opposite [[odd-pinnate]] green leaves, with 3 to 13 serrate, 8- to 10-cm-long leaflets. The leaflets, [[Glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]] on both sides, have a [[lanceolate]] blade 2–10 cm long and 1–4 cm wide, with a long acuminate apex and a wedge-shaped base.

The large, showy, golden yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers are in clusters at the ends of branches. The [[petal|corolla]] of the flower is bell- to funnel-shaped, five-lobed (weakly two-lipped), often reddish-veined in the throat and is 3.5 to 8.5 cm long. Flowering takes place from spring to fall, but more profusely from spring to summer.<ref>[https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Tecoma~stans#:~:text=Flowering%3A%20spring%E2%80%93summer.,%2C%20Mexico%2C%20Peru%20%26%20Ecuador. Tecoma stans (L.) Kunth] NEW SOUTH WALES FLORA ONLINE. PlantNet. Retrieved 26 July 2023.</ref><ref>[https://www.gardenia.net/plant/tecoma-stans Tecoma Stans (Yellow Bells)] Gardenia.net. Retrieved 26 July 2023.</ref> 

The fruits, narrow [[capsule (fruit)|capsules]], arise from two [[carpel]]s and are up to 25 cm long. A fruit contains many yellow seeds with membranopus wings; when the fruit opens upon ripening, these seed are spread by the wind ([[anemochory]]). The flowers attract [[bee]]s, [[butterfly|butterflies]], and [[hummingbird]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mendonça |first1=Luciana Baza |last2=Anjos |first2=Luiz dos |title=Beija-flores (Aves, Trochilidae) e seus recursos florais em uma área urbana do Sul do Brasil |trans-title=Hummingbirds (Aves, Trochilidae) and their flowers in an urban area of southern Brazil |language=pt |journal=Revista Brasileira de Zoologia |date=March 2005 |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=51–59 |doi=10.1590/S0101-81752005000100007 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Apart from sexually by seed, ''Tecoma stans'' can also be reproduced asexually by stem [[cuttings (plant)|cuttings]].

==Habitat==
''Tecoma stans'' is native to the [[Americas]]. It extends from the [[southern United States]] through Mexico, [[Central America]], and the [[Antilles]] to northern Venezuela, and through the [[Andes]] mountain range to northern Argentina. It was introduced in [[southern Africa]], [[India]], and [[Hawaii]]. It is evergreen in moist and warmer regions, but is [[deciduous]] in more temperate regions that have a pronounced dry season.<ref name=cabi>[https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/10.1079/cabicompendium.52951 Tecoma stans (yellow bells)] by [[Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International]]. Retrieved 27 May 2024.</ref>

Yellow trumpetbush is a [[ruderal species]], readily colonizing disturbed, rocky, [[sand]]y, and cleared land and occasionally becoming an [[invasive weed]]. It thrives in a wide variety of ecosystems, from high altitude [[temperate forest]]s and tropical deciduous and evergreen forests, to [[xerophilous]] scrub and the intertropical [[littoral]]. It quickly colonizes disturbed, rocky, sandy, and cleared fields. The species prefers dry and sunny regions of the coast.<ref name=cabi/>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Pollination in Tecoma stans by Honey Bee (cropped).jpg|thumb|right|Pollination of the plant by a honey bee]]
''Tecoma stans'' is drought-tolerant and grows well in warm climates. It is cultivated as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]]. They are grown in many parts of the world for their beautiful flowering, to adorn streets and gardens. It can be easily propagated by stem [[cuttings (plant)|cuttings]]. Native to the southwestern United States and adjacent Mexico, ''Tecoma stans var. angustata'' is shorter and more tolerant of drought and cold than many of the tropical varieties commonly sold in nurseries.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tecoma stans (Yellow bells) |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=test |website=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center |publisher=University of Texas at Austin |access-date=5 July 2026}}</ref>

===Uses===
The wood of ''Tecoma stans'' is used in rustic architecture like [[bahareque]], for the construction of furniture and canoes, or as [[firewood]] or charcoal. It is a [[medicinal plant]] used against [[diabetes]] and against diseases of the [[digestive system]], among other uses. The plant is desirable [[fodder]] when it grows in fields grazed by [[livestock]]. 

It is a very potent anti-venom against [[cobra]] [[snake venom|venom]], used by Pakistani old medicine. It is proved to be better than [[antiserum]], the paste of this plant's leaves are applied topically on the cobra bite. Its bio-chemicals bind with the cobra venom [[enzyme]]s thus effectively inhibiting the venom.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Asad |first1=Muhammad Hassham Hassan Bin |last2=Murtaza |first2=Ghulam |last3=Ubaid |first3=Muhammad |last4=Sajjad |first4=Ashif |last5=Mehmood |first5=Rubada |last6=Mahmood |first6=Qaisar |last7=Ansari |first7=Muhammad Muzzmil |last8=Karim |first8=Sabiha |last9=Mehmood |first9=Zahid |last10=Hussain |first10=Izhar |last11=Hussain |first11=I |title=Naja naja karachiensis Envenomation: Biochemical Parameters for Cardiac, Liver, and Renal Damage along with Their Neutralization by Medicinal Plants |journal=BioMed Research International |date=2014 |volume=2014 |article-number=970540 |doi=10.1155/2014/970540 |pmid=24877153 |pmc=4022246 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

''Tecoma stans'' is unique in that although it is nontoxic itself, the honey from its flowers is poisonous nonetheless.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anand |first1=Mukul |last2=Basavaraju |first2=R. |title=A review on phytochemistry and pharmacological uses of Tecoma stans (L.) Juss. ex Kunth |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |date=January 2021 |volume=265 |article-number=113270 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2020.113270 |pmid=32822823 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first1=K |last1=Pallavi |first2=B |last2=Vishnavi |last3=Mamatha |first4=K Vanitha |last4=Prakash |first5=A |last5=Amruthapriyanka |title=Phytochemical investigation and anti-microbial activity of Tecoma stans |journal=World Journal of Pharmaceutical Research |volume=3 |issue=2 |date=2014 |pages=2070–2083 |url=https://www.wjpr.net/abstract_show/633 }}</ref>

==Invasiveness==
''Tecoma stans'' has invasive potential and occasionally becomes a weed. The species is considered invasive in Africa (especially South Africa), South America, Asia, Australia and the [[Pacific Islands]]. It now presents a significant danger for biodiversity. It competes with local species and can form thick, almost monospecific [[thicket]]s. Seedlings establish speedily with a prominent [[tap root]]. The tree can replant from cut roots, thereby causing rapid re-infestation unless the remaining roots are burnt off.<ref name=cabi/>
